Going Deeper | James Worthy James Worthy built his reputation on rising to the moment, and few stages were bigger than the 1982 NCAA Tournament. Playing under Dean Smith alongside future NBA stars Michael Jordan and Sam Perkins, Worthy was the steady force that powered North Carolina through the Final Four. A North Carolina native, Worthy delivered when it mattered most. In the national semifinal, the Tar Heels took down a talented Houston team to advance to the championship. Two nights later, Worthy put together one of the defining performances of the tournament, scoring 28 points and earning Most Outstanding Player honors as North Carolina defeated Georgetown for the title. That stretch wasn’t just a hot streak, it was a glimpse of what was coming. Worthy’s combination of size, fluidity, and composure made him one of the most complete players in the country, and it ultimately led to him being selected first overall in the 1982 NBA Draft by the Los Angeles Lakers. In the NBA, he became “Big Game James” for a reason. Worthy thrived in high-pressure moments, helping lead the Lakers to three championships and earning Finals MVP honors in 1988. His ability to deliver on the biggest stage became his trademark.

title: Patrick Ewing New York Knicks 1995-1996 Game Worn Jersey | Matched to 2 Games | 31 Points | Double-Double | 4 Blocks
description_block: Few uniforms in professional basketball carry the weight of the New York Knicks blue away jersey. It is a design that belongs to the city as much as the team, instantly recognizable, loaded with history, and worn by some of the greatest players the sport has ever produced. This example was worn in two games by Patrick Ewing, the player considered the greatest Knick of all time, during the peak of his career in the 1995-1996 NBA season. It is an important and rare piece of Knicks memorabilia. Patrick Ewing and New York were inseparable. At seven feet tall, he was a towering figure among the skyscrapers of Manhattan, a physical and symbolic presence who carried the Knicks on his back for a decade and a half. He arrived in 1985 as the first overall pick and spent 15 of his 17 career seasons in blue and orange, becoming the franchise in every meaningful sense. There was no Knicks basketball without Patrick Ewing. He was the engine of their greatest runs, the face of their toughest losses, and the standard against which every player who wore that uniform after him would be measured. The blue away jersey offered here was worn in two games during the 1995-1996 season, a year in which Ewing remained one of the most dominant big men in the league at 33 years old. The first came on December 22, 1995, when the Knicks traveled to Orlando to face the Magic. The Magic were in the middle of their Shaquille O'Neal and Penny Hardaway era, a genuine powerhouse in the Eastern Conference, and the game reflected that. Ewing finished with 13 points, 9 rebounds, 1 assist, and 4 blocks in a losing effort, as the Magic won convincingly, 111-90. The 4 blocks speak to something that statistics rarely captured fully about Ewing: even on nights when the offense was not flowing, his presence in the paint altered the game. He was a deterrent as much as a scorer, and Orlando's size made for one of the more physically demanding matchups of the season. The second game was a different story entirely. On February 28, 1996, the Knicks hosted the Sacramento Kings, and Ewing turned in the kind of performance that reminded everyone why he remained one of the most feared players in the league. He finished with 31 points, 13 rebounds, 3 assists, and 1 block, a double-double that carried the Knicks almost entirely on his shoulders. He scored 31 of New York's 85 points, a staggering share of the offensive load, in a narrow 90-85 loss to the Kings. It was a signature Ewing performance in the truest sense: relentless, physical, and dominant even in defeat. Those were the nights that defined his career in New York, games where he willed the team into contention through sheer force and refused to let them be put away easily. The blue away jersey itself is part of what makes this piece so significant. The Knicks road uniform of this era, with its deep royal blue, the clean white lettering, and the timeless block font, is among the most iconic designs in American sports. It carries the weight of Madison Square Garden, of playoff battles against the Bulls and the Pacers and the Heat, of a generation of basketball played in the most demanding market in the country. When people picture Patrick Ewing, they often picture him in this jersey, jaw set, backing down into the post, the Garden rising around him. Going Deeper | Patrick Ewing At seven feet tall, Patrick Ewing was a towering figure among the skyscrapers of New York City, where he played 15 of his 17 career seasons for the New York Knicks. The legendary Hall of Famer is an 11-time NBA All-Star with 2 Olympic Gold Medals. His incredible skills led him to achieve more than 24,000 points and 11,000 rebounds, and he was named to the 50 Greatest Players in NBA History list in 1996. Over his incredible career, Ewing averaged 21 points, 9.8 rebounds, and 1.9 assists per game. To own this jersey is to own a piece of that legacy, a garment worn in by one of the greatest players in the history of one of professional basketball's most storied franchises, in the uniform that defined an era.

title: Stephen Curry Golden State Warriors 2016 NBA Finals Game Worn Signed and Inscribed Sneakers | Games 3 & 4
description_block: These sneakers were worn by Stephen Curry during Games 3 and 4 of the 2016 NBA Finals, the culmination of one of the most celebrated seasons in NBA history. That year, the Golden State Warriors set the all-time regular season record with 73 wins, surpassing the 1995-96 Chicago Bulls' 72-win mark, and Curry was named the NBA's first unanimous MVP in league history. What followed was the most dramatic comeback in Finals history. LeBron James and Kyrie Irving each scored 41 points in Game 5, James scored 41 again in Game 6, and in a tense Game 7 at Oracle Arena, James delivered a chase-down block on Andre Iguodala with under two minutes remaining and the score tied, before Irving hit a go-ahead three-pointer over Curry with 53 seconds left to seal a 93-89 Cavaliers victory. Cleveland became the first and only team to overcome a 3-1 series deficit in the NBA Finals, ending a 52-year championship drought in the city. In Game 3, the Cavaliers delivered a statement victory, routing the Warriors 120-90 at Quicken Loans Arena to get on the board, with Curry recording 19 points, 3 assists, and 2 steals in 31 minutes. Curry wore these sneakers in the second half of Game 3. Two nights later in Game 4, Curry responded with one of his finest performances of the series, scoring 38 points to give the Warriors a seemingly insurmountable 3-1 lead. That the series would ultimately unfold as it did only deepens the historical resonance of these sneakers, artifacts of a Finals that redefined what was possible in championship basketball. title: Julius “Dr. J” Erving 1978 NBA All-Star Ring
description_block: Originally presented to Julius Erving to honor his appearance in the 1978 NBA All-Star Game and later passed on to his son, Julius Erving III, the provenance of this ring is as remarkable as the man it honors. By February of 1978, Erving was already one of the biggest stars in professional basketball. In his first NBA All-Star appearance the year prior, he had put up 30 points and won All-Star Game MVP, announcing himself to the NBA stage in emphatic fashion after years of dominance in the ABA. The 1978 game was only his second NBA All-Star appearance, yet he arrived in Atlanta as the most voted-in player in the Eastern Conference, a reflection of just how quickly he had captured the imagination of a new fan base. That season he would go on to earn All-NBA First Team honors, cementing his status as one of the premier players in the league. He delivered on All-Star night as well, finishing with 16 points, 8 rebounds, 3 assists, and 1 block as the East topped the West 133-125, with Dr. J's performance at the heart of the victory. The ring is set in classic All-Star fashion, a ball mounted in black stone, and features the Atlanta Hawks logo in tribute to the host city. It is an increasingly rare surviving artifact from Dr. J's playing days, a physical connection to a moment when one of basketball's most electric talents was at the height of his powers and at the center of the sport's growing national spotlight. Kept within the Erving family before making its way to auction in 2009, this is the kind of piece that rarely surfaces, a ring honoring and given directly to the man who wore it and the performance he delivered that night in Atlanta. The ring is accompanied by a signed letter from Julius Erving III in regards to the provenance. Going Deeper | Julius Erving To understand what Julius Erving meant to basketball, it helps to understand what the game looked like before him. The dunk existed, but it belonged to the big men, used for power and proximity. What Erving did was something different entirely. He launched from distance, gathered in the air, and finished with a creativity and grace that the sport had never seen. He did not just dunk. He invented a new language for what a basketball player could be. Erving built his legend first in the ABA, a league that embraced the kind of above-the-rim play that the NBA had not yet fully welcomed. With the Virginia Squires and then the New York Nets, he won two championships, four MVP awards across both leagues, and three scoring titles, while drawing fans to a league that desperately needed a marquee star. When the ABA merged with the NBA in 1976, Erving came with it, joining the Philadelphia 76ers and immediately becoming one of the faces of the sport at a pivotal moment in its growth. His highlight reel from those years remains remarkable decades later. The 1976 ABA Slam Dunk Contest, where he soared from the free-throw line and seemed to hang in the air longer than physics should allow. The baseline move against the Lakers in the 1980 NBA Finals, where he went under the backboard and flipped the ball in from the other side in a single fluid motion. The "Rock the Baby" dunk. These were not just athletic feats. They were moments that expanded what people believed was possible on a basketball court. The hardware followed. He was named NBA MVP in 1981 and two years later led the 76ers to the championship, sweeping the defending champion Los Angeles Lakers in four games. Across his 16 professional seasons, his teams never once missed the postseason. He finished his career with 30,026 combined ABA and NBA points, ninth all-time across both leagues. Erving was inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame in 1993 and was named to the NBA's 50th and 75th Anniversary Teams. Sports Illustrated named him one of the 40 most important athletes of all time in 1994. But the numbers and the honors only tell part of the story. The term "posterized," the idea of a dunk so decisive it belongs on a poster, was coined in his image. The slam dunk as art form, as a legitimate and graceful weapon rather than mere spectacle, is his legacy as much as anyone's. He did not just play the game at a high level. He changed what the game was.

Going Deeper - Giannis Antetokounmpo Nicknamed the ‘Greek Freak’ because of his home country and freakish athleticism, Giannis Antetokounmpo is arguably the league’s most dominant player. Antetokounmpo’s resume is already Hall of Fame worthy. He won back-to-back league MVPs in 2018-2019 and 2019-2020. He was also named Defensive Player of the Year in the later season. Following the 2020-2021 season, Giannis added an NBA Finals MVP and All-Star Game MVP to his trophy case. His 50-point and 14-rebound performance in the series-clinching Game 6 of the 2021 NBA Finals is one of the greatest individual NBA Finals game performances of all time. Antetokounmpo is a 10-time NBA All-Star, a 7-time All-NBA 1st Team member, a 2-time All-NBA 2nd Team member, and has been named to 5 NBA All-Defensive Teams. Going Deeper | Steph Curry Selected by the Golden State Warriors as the 7th overall pick of the 2009 NBA Draft, Curry quickly emerged as an elite scoring and playmaking threat as a point guard. He averaged 17.5 points, 5.9 assists, and 4.5 rebounds and finished second in the Rookie of the Year award voting. Although Curry’s skillset and potential shined bright, the Warriors failed to make the playoffs in his first three seasons. This all changed after the Warriors drafted shooting guard Klay Thompson in 2011. Soon thereafter, Curry and Thompson emerged as the most dangerous shooting backcourt in the game and were dubbed the ‘Splash Brothers’. After two consecutive playoff appearances in 2012-2013 and 2013-2014, Curry and the Warriors finally broke through in the 2014-15 NBA Playoffs. The Warriors’ balanced offensive attack of Curry, Thompson, Draymond Green, and Andre Iguodala enabled them to defeat LeBron James and the Cleveland Cavaliers for the franchise’s first championship since the 1974-1975 season. In addition, Curry was voted league MVP. Curry has helped the Warriors win three more championships in 2017, 2018, and 2022. His career accomplishments to date include eleven All-NBA selections, two MVPs, one Finals MVP, two scoring titles, and being named to the 75th Anniversary Team. The NBA 75th Anniversary Team was selected by a blue-ribbon panel of players, coaches, general managers, and sportswriters who voted on the 75 Greatest Players in NBA History. Only 11 active players were selected for the team, including Stephen Curry. In 2021, Curry passed Ray Allen to become the all-time leader in three-pointers in NBA history. He is widely considered perhaps the greatest shooter and one of the best players of all time. Curry played a major role in Team USA’s run to a gold medal in the 2024 Paris Olympics. He hit huge shots down the stretch in the Gold Medal game against France, quelling any French hopes of a comeback victory on home soil. This was Curry’s first, and likely only, Olympic gold medal with Team USA. At the time of cataloging, Curry holds career averages of 24.8 points, 4.7 rebounds, and 6.3 assists per game. A two-time MVP, four-time champion, and perennial All-NBA selection, Curry’s sustained excellence and longevity continue to define an era of basketball history.

Going Deeper - Shai Gilgeous-Alexander Shai Gilgeous-Alexander won MVP for the 2024-2025 NBA season and led his team to the NBA Championship. Shai was selected as an All-Star starter in only his 3rd ever All-Star appearance. As the Thunder mark their first championship in Oklahoma and only their second in franchise history, with Shai Gilgeous-Alexander as their indisputable star, Gilgeous-Alexander and the Thunder look to forge the latest NBA dynasty. Drafted 11th overall in the 2018 NBA Draft, Gilgeous-Alexander began his career with the Los Angeles Clippers. He quickly showcased his remarkable ball-handling and defensive abilities, with his play securing him a spot on the NBA All-Rookie 2nd Team. In a consequential 2019 trade, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander was moved to the Oklahoma City Thunder as part of a deal involving Paul George. He thrived in his new expanded role and displayed significant versatility, contributing significantly in scoring, playmaking, and defensive efforts. In 2023, Shai’s ascent in the NBA reached new heights when he earned his first All-Star selection and was named to the All-NBA First Team. His consistent excellence has firmly established him as one of the premier talents in the league with the potential to define the next NBA era. title: Set of Two | Nike Zoom Kobe IV and Zoom Kobe V "Think Pink" Promo Samples, Sizes 6 and 7
description_block: Offered here as a single lot are two unreleased Nike Basketball promo samples produced in the "Think Pink" colorway: a 2008 Nike Zoom Kobe IV in size 6 and a 2009 Nike Zoom Kobe V in size 7, both produced in tribute to the Kay Yow Cancer Fund. Together, the two pairs document consecutive chapters of the Think Pink initiative across Kobe's signature line, spanning the back-to-back championship seasons of 2008-09 and 2009-10.

The triumph not only delivered his maiden Australian Open crown but also established him as the youngest player in history to complete the career Grand Slam, cementing his place among the sport’s all-time elite. As the opening Grand Slam of the season, the Australian Open has long provided the stage for tennis’ most enduring moments. The 2026 championship stands among the tournament’s most significant, pairing one of the greatest champions in history against the sport’s brightest young star in a final that marked the beginning of a new chapter in men’s tennis.
